title: Why Is the Donbas Front Line Stuck?

minor: 'Most of this front sits on flat coal-country steppe': the 1,200 km front also runs through Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia, which are not coal country. Say 'Most of Donbas sits on...' or 'the Donbas part of this front'.
The cold open's figures (1,200 km, under 1 percent in 2024, 4,000-4,300 km²) cover the whole front, but the question that follows is about Donbas only. Say so aloud, e.g. 'across the whole front'.

'The second is Russia's demand: Ukraine pulls back to the edge of Donetsk region' drops the earlier attribution. The source is Reuters citing sources, and the Kremlin has not confirmed it. Use 'Reuters says Russia's demand is...'.

Unsourced assertions: 'tree lines are often the only cover for kilometres', the Siverskyi Donets as 'a natural barrier in every battle', 'each one can take months of fighting to cross', 'For eight years both sides dug in... trenches, bunkers and minefields', and 'a claim almost no other country recognises'. Add sources or soften them.
'Ukraine's only coking coal mine': the source supports 'the only one in Ukrainian-held territory' or 'its main one'. Check the wording.
Zelensky's 9 August quote comes after the 15 August Anchorage line, so the order is reversed. Say 'Days before the summit, Zelensky said...'.
The Pokrovsk coking-coal line comes without any map link to the Donetsk fortress-belt cities, so it reads as a non sequitur. Link it to the cities or the front.

shots.vo: Donbas usually means two Ukrainian regions, Donetsk and Luhansk, on the border with Russia, plus fringes of their neighbours.
The two regions together cover about 53,000 square kilometres, a little larger than the whole of Costa Rica.
Before 2014, about six and a half million people lived here, Ukraine's statistics service said.

shots.vo: Its mines and steel mills made it Ukraine's industrial heart, about 15 percent of the economy in 2013.
By late 2025, Russian forces held nearly all of Luhansk and most of Donetsk, ISW maps showed.
Ukraine still held or defended a chain of cities in northern Donetsk: Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka.
From the city of Donetsk to Kramatorsk is only about 80 kilometres in a straight line.
Now look at the ground itself, because it explains much of why this front is stuck.
Most of Donbas is open steppe: wide, flat fields broken only by thin rows of trees.

Coal mining also left tall slag heaps, man-made hills that give anyone on top a long view.

shots.vo: The town that grew around the works was named Yuzovka, later Stalino, and renamed Donetsk in 1961.
After the revolution, Moscow drew a border between Soviet Ukraine and Soviet Russia right through this coal field.

Soviet planners later lined these fields with windbreaks of trees, rows like those soldiers fight from today.
In 2001, Ukraine's census found 57 percent of Donetsk region's people were Ukrainian and 38 percent Russian.
Yet in December 1991, about 84 percent of voters in both regions backed Ukraine's independence.
That vote turned an internal Soviet line into an international border, with Donbas inside Ukraine.
In early 2014, protests in Kyiv toppled President Viktor Yanukovych, who fled to Russia.
That April, armed separatists seized government buildings in Sloviansk, Donetsk and Luhansk.
Ukraine and Western governments said Russia armed and led them; Moscow denied sending its troops.

By early July 2022, Russia had taken Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk, and with them almost all of Luhansk.
In September 2022, Russia held votes in occupied areas and declared four Ukrainian regions annexed.
Around then Ukraine struck back, retaking most of Kharkiv region and, on 1 October, the town of Lyman.
On 12 October, the UN General Assembly rejected the annexation by 143 votes to 5.

shots.vo: Over that winter, Russian forces dug belts of trenches, anti-tank ditches and minefields across the south and east.
When Ukraine attacked in June 2023, its columns slowed in those minefields and freed only a handful of villages.
In Donbas itself, the battle for Bakhmut lasted about ten months, until Russia claimed it in May 2023.
In February 2024, Ukraine withdrew from Avdiivka, a town about 15 kilometres north of central Donetsk.
Since 2023, the changes have come one town at a time, each costing months of fighting.
Within months the front crept west about 40 kilometres, to the edges of Pokrovsk.
Both sides have paid heavily for every one of those kilometres. So what does each one say it wants?
Russia's constitution now lists Donetsk and Luhansk as Russian regions, a claim almost no other country recognises.
Moscow says President Viktor Yanukovych was removed unconstitutionally in 2014, and Putin called it an armed seizure of power.

shots.vo: For Russia, the part of Donetsk region it does not hold is land it already calls its own.
Russia also outspends Ukraine: about 149 billion dollars on its military in 2024, against 65 billion, SIPRI estimates.
But Ukraine's figure was about 34 percent of its whole economy, and Western military aid adds to it.
Analysts at ISW call those northern cities Ukraine's fortress belt; beyond them lies Dnipro, about 190 kilometres west.
Pokrovsk also held Ukraine's only coking coal mine, which Metinvest halted in January 2025 as fighting neared.
On 15 August 2025, US President Donald Trump met Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, but no ceasefire was agreed.
Reuters reported that Russia asked Ukraine to leave the rest of Donetsk in return for freezing other fronts.
Zelensky said on 9 August: Ukrainians will not gift their land to the occupier.

shots.vo: In November 2025, a US draft peace plan, reported by Axios and Reuters, proposed a demilitarised zone in that same area.
Every draft hits the same question: who holds the land between the armies? There are three ways it could go.
The first is a ceasefire along today's line, freezing the front roughly where the armies now stand.
Korea did that in 1953, along an armistice line about 250 kilometres long.
Ukraine's front, by Syrskyi's count of about 1,200 kilometres, is nearly five times longer than Korea's.
On the map, a freeze would make the front a border in practice, though not in law, with both claims kept.

map.label: A border in practice, not in law

shots.vo: The second is Russia's demand: Ukraine pulls back to the edge of Donetsk region, moving the line west.

shots.vo: That would hand over Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, cities home to more than 250,000 people before the war.
Analysts say Ukraine's next line would sit on open farmland to the west, with fewer hills and towns to hold.

map.label: Open ground beyond the region border (ISW)

shots.vo: Kyiv fears a springboard for the next attack; Moscow says the land is Russian by its law.
The third is no deal at all, and the slow grind goes on, a few villages at a time.
Analysts at RUSI say either side could still break through if the other runs short of soldiers, shells or air defence.

In Donbas, drawing a line on a map takes a minute; moving one now takes armies a year.
